decks.title: Solutions and Their Concentration — Part 1: Types of solutions, concentration and gas solubility
goals: Classify solutions by the states of solute and solvent, including solid solutions
Calculate mass percentage, ppm, mole fraction, molarity, molality and normality, and convert between them
Explain why molality, unlike molarity, does not change with temperature
Apply Henry’s law and explain its everyday applications

slides.heading: Solutions and their concentration
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a solution is, how strong it is, and how much gas a liquid can hold.

visual.alt: Flow: a solute and a solvent form a homogeneous solution, whose strength is given by concentration terms and whose gas content follows Henry’s law

slides.narration: Namaste! An injection of saline, a bottle of soda, the coolant in a car and the brass of a door handle are all solutions. A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. In this part we learn the different types of solution, the many ways of stating how concentrated a solution is, and how pressure controls the amount of gas that dissolves in a liquid.

slides.heading: Types of solutions
slides.body_md: The component present in the larger amount is the **solvent**; the others are **solutes**. The solvent decides the physical state. **Solid solutions** include alloys such as brass and amalgams.

visual.alt: Table of the nine types of solution by the state of the solvent and the solute, with an example of each

slides.narration: Look at the table. The solvent sets the state of the solution, and the solute can be a gas, a liquid or a solid. Air is a gaseous solution, soda water a liquid solution of a gas, and brass a solid solution of zinc in copper. Solid solutions are common in everyday metals: the gold in jewellery is usually alloyed with copper or silver. In every case the mixture is uniform all through.

slides.heading: Percentages and parts per million
slides.body_md: Percentages and **parts per million** suit labels and very dilute solutions.

rows: grams of solute per 100 mL of solution

visual.alt: Table of mass percentage, volume percentage, mass by volume percentage and parts per million with definitions and uses

slides.narration: Labels often state concentration as a percentage. Mass percentage compares masses, volume percentage compares volumes, and mass by volume percentage gives grams of solute in a hundred millilitres of solution. For traces, such as fluoride in drinking water or lead in soil, we use parts per million: grams of the trace substance in a million grams of the mixture. One ppm is a milligram in a kilogram.

slides.heading: Mole fraction, molarity and molality
slides.body_md: Mole-based units count particles. Molality and mole fraction use **masses only**, so they do **not** change with temperature; molarity uses the **volume of solution**, which expands on heating.

visual.alt: Table giving the formula, unit and temperature dependence of mole fraction, molarity and molality

slides.narration: Three mole-based units appear in almost every numerical. Mole fraction is the share of all the moles that belong to one component, and the fractions add up to one. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Because a liquid expands when warmed, molarity falls slightly on heating, while molality, built only from masses, stays the same.

slides.heading: Normality and gram equivalents
slides.body_md: **Normality** $N$ is the number of **gram equivalents** of solute per litre of solution. Equivalent mass $=$ molar mass $\div\ n$, where $n$ is the basicity of an acid, the acidity of a base, or the number of electrons gained or lost per formula unit in a redox reaction. So $N = n \times M$.

visual.alt: Table of molar mass, n-factor and equivalent mass for some acids, bases and potassium permanganate

math: N = \dfrac{\text{gram equivalents of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in L}}
slides.narration: Normality counts equivalents instead of moles. An equivalent of an acid is the amount that supplies one mole of hydrogen ions; for sulfuric acid, which gives two, the equivalent mass is half the molar mass. So a one molar sulfuric acid solution is two normal. Normality is handy in titrations, because at the end point the equivalents of acid and base are equal, which gives the relation N one V one equals N two V two.

slides.heading: Worked example: molality, mole fraction and ppm
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $27\ \text{g}$ of glucose ($M = 180$) is dissolved in $250\ \text{g}$ of water. Find (a) the molality and (b) the mole fraction of glucose. (c) A water sample contains $0.6\ \text{mg}$ of fluoride in $500\ \text{g}$. Express this in ppm.

**(a)** Moles of glucose $= 27 \div 180 = 0.15$; molality $= 0.15 \div 0.250 = 0.60\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

**(b)** Moles of water $= 250 \div 18 = 13.89$; $x = 0.15 \div (0.15 + 13.89) = 0.0107$.

**(c)** ppm $= \dfrac{0.6 \times 10^{-3}}{500} \times 10^{6} = 1.2\ \text{ppm}$.

visual.alt: Table of the results of the worked example

slides.narration: Convert masses to moles first. Twenty seven grams of glucose is nought point one five mole, and two hundred and fifty grams of water is nearly fourteen mole. Divide the glucose moles by the mass of water in kilograms to get the molality, nought point six. Divide by the total moles for the mole fraction. For ppm, divide the mass of fluoride by the mass of the sample and multiply by a million.

slides.heading: Worked example: normality and molarity of an acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sulfuric acid solution is $24.5\%$ by mass with density $1.20\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$ ($M = 98$). Find its molarity and normality, and the volume needed to neutralise $50\ \text{mL}$ of $0.60\ \text{N}$ NaOH.

**Step 1.** In $100\ \text{g}$: $24.5\ \text{g}$ acid $= 24.5 \div 98 = 0.25\ \text{mol}$; volume $= 100 \div 1.20 = 83.3\ \text{mL}$.

**Step 2.** Molarity $= 0.25 \div 0.0833 = 3.0\ \text{M}$; normality $= 2 \times 3.0 = 6.0\ \text{N}$.

**Step 3.** $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$: $V_1 = 0.60 \times 50 \div 6.0 = 5.0\ \text{mL}$.

visual.alt: Flow for converting a mass percentage into molarity and normality and then using N1V1 = N2V2

slides.narration: Imagine exactly one hundred grams of solution. It holds twenty four and a half grams of acid, a quarter of a mole. Density turns a hundred grams into about eighty three millilitres, so the molarity is three. Sulfuric acid is dibasic, so the normality is twice that, six. For the titration, equivalents of acid equal equivalents of base, so only five millilitres of this strong acid are needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: which unit ignores temperature?
slides.body_md: A solution is made up at 15 °C and used at 35 °C. Which concentration term is unchanged?
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask which terms are built from masses alone and which need the volume of the solution.

slides.heading: Gases in liquids: the role of pressure
slides.body_md: Raising the pressure of a gas above a liquid drives more gas particles into the liquid until a new equilibrium is reached, so the solubility of a gas **increases with pressure**. It **decreases** as temperature rises, because dissolving a gas is usually exothermic.

slides.narration: Picture a gas trapped above water in a cylinder. Gas particles keep striking the surface and some dissolve. Push the piston down, and the squeezed gas strikes the surface more often, so more dissolves until escaping and dissolving balance again. Warming does the opposite: dissolving a gas usually gives out heat, so a warm liquid holds less gas, which is why a warm soda goes flat faster.

slides.heading: Henry’s law
slides.body_md: **Henry’s law:** at constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above it. In the mole-fraction form, $p = K_\text{H}\, x$. A **larger** $K_\text{H}$ means a **less** soluble gas; $K_\text{H}$ rises with temperature.

visual.alt: Table of Henry’s law constants in water for helium, nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Henry’s law says that, at a fixed temperature, the amount of gas that dissolves is proportional to its partial pressure. In symbols, partial pressure equals Henry’s constant times the mole fraction of the gas in solution. A large constant means a large pressure is needed to dissolve even a little gas, so helium, with a huge constant, is far less soluble than carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Worked example: oxygen dissolved in a fish tank
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Air contains oxygen at a partial pressure of $0.21\ \text{bar}$. With $K_\text{H}(\ce{O2}) = 34.86\ \text{kbar}$ at $293\ \text{K}$, estimate the mass of oxygen dissolved in $1.0\ \text{kg}$ of aquarium water.

**Step 1.** $x_{\ce{O2}} = p \div K_\text{H} = 0.21 \div 34860 = 6.02 \times 10^{-6}$.

**Step 2.** Moles of water $= 1000 \div 18 = 55.6$; $n_{\ce{O2}} \approx x \times n_\text{water} = 3.35 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 3.** Mass $= 3.35 \times 10^{-4} \times 32 = 0.0107\ \text{g}$, about $10.7\ \text{mg}$ per kg.

visual.alt: Flow for a Henry’s law calculation from partial pressure to mass of dissolved gas

slides.narration: Put both pressures in bar first: thirty four point eight six kilobar is thirty four thousand eight hundred and sixty bar. Dividing the partial pressure by this constant gives a tiny mole fraction, about six millionths. A kilogram of water is about fifty six mole, so roughly a third of a millimole of oxygen dissolves, about eleven milligrams. That small amount is all the oxygen the fish can breathe.

slides.heading: Henry’s law in daily life
slides.body_md: Henry’s law explains several everyday and medical effects.

rows: CO₂ is sealed in under high pressure
High pressure raises solubility; opening the bottle releases gas
Nitrogen dissolves in blood at depth; rising fast forms bubbles (the bends)
Tanks use air diluted with helium, which is less soluble
Low partial pressure of O₂, so less dissolves in blood
KH rises with temperature, so less O₂ dissolves

visual.alt: Table of four situations explained by Henry’s law

slides.narration: Henry’s law is all around you. Soft drinks are bottled under high pressure of carbon dioxide and fizz when opened. Divers who rise too quickly suffer the bends, as nitrogen dissolved under pressure forms bubbles in the blood, so their tanks use air diluted with helium. At high altitude less oxygen dissolves in the blood, and on hot afternoons ponds hold too little oxygen for fish.

slides.body_md: Use Henry’s constants or the effect of pressure and temperature to compare gas solubilities.
slides.narration: Quick check. The larger the Henry’s constant, the larger the pressure needed to dissolve the same amount of gas.

slides.body_md: Relate normality to molarity for an acid or a base.
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply the molarity by the number of replaceable hydrogen ions or hydroxide ions.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Nine types of solution by states of solvent and solute; alloys and amalgams are solid solutions.
Mass %, volume %, w/v %, ppm, mole fraction, molarity, molality and normality.
Normality = n × molarity; N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ at the end point of a titration.
Mole fraction, mass % and molality do not change with temperature; molarity and normality do.
Henry’s law $p = K_\text{H}\,x$: gas solubility rises with pressure and falls with temperature.

visual.alt: Summary table of concentration terms and Henry’s law

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Solutions can be gaseous, liquid or solid. Their strength can be stated in many ways, from percentages and parts per million to mole fraction, molarity, molality and normality, and you can convert between them. Mass-based terms do not change with temperature. And Henry’s law tells us that gases dissolve more under higher pressure and less in warmer liquids.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Molality uses kg of **solvent**: subtract the solute’s mass first.
When a percentage and a density are given, assume 100 g of solution.
For normality, state the n-factor (basicity, acidity or electrons transferred).
In Henry’s law, use the same pressure unit for $p$ and $K_\text{H}$ (1 kbar = 1000 bar).

rows: Dividing by kg of solution for molality

visual.alt: Table of common slips in Part 1 and how to fix them

slides.narration: Some quick tips. For molality divide by the mass of solvent, not of solution. Imagine one hundred grams whenever a percentage comes with a density. Always state the n-factor when you use normality. And keep pressure units the same in Henry’s law, remembering that a larger constant means a less soluble gas.

decks.title: Solutions and Their Concentration — Part 2: Raoult’s law, non-ideal solutions and azeotropes
goals: Apply Raoult’s law to a mixture of two volatile liquids and to a solution of a non-volatile solute
Compare ideal and non-ideal solutions in terms of intermolecular forces, enthalpy and volume of mixing
Distinguish minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes with examples and graphs
Explain why an azeotrope cannot be separated by fractional distillation

slides.heading: Vapour pressure of solutions
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the vapour above a mixture of liquids behaves, and why some mixtures cannot be separated by distillation.

visual.alt: Flow from Raoult’s law to ideal solutions, deviations and azeotropes

slides.narration: When a liquid evaporates in a closed space, its vapour exerts a pressure called the vapour pressure. In this part we see how the vapour pressure of a mixture depends on its composition, why some mixtures follow a simple law and others do not, and why a distillery cannot get pure ethanol simply by distilling a mixture of ethanol and water.

slides.heading: Raoult’s law for two volatile liquids
slides.body_md: In a mixture of volatile liquids A and B, **each partial vapour pressure is proportional to the mole fraction** of that liquid. By Dalton’s law the total pressure is the sum. The vapour is **richer in the more volatile** component.

visual.alt: Flow from liquid mole fractions to partial pressures, total pressure and vapour composition

math: p_\text{A} = p^\circ_\text{A}\, x_\text{A}, \qquad p_\text{B} = p^\circ_\text{B}\, x_\text{B}
slides.narration: Raoult’s law says each liquid’s partial vapour pressure equals its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction in the mixture. Adding the partial pressures gives the total, by Dalton’s law. Dividing one partial pressure by the total gives that component’s share of the vapour. Because the more volatile liquid escapes more readily, the vapour always contains more of it than the liquid does.

slides.heading: Raoult’s law on a graph
slides.body_md: For an ideal solution, both partial pressures and the total pressure are **straight lines** against composition.

x.label: Mole fraction of B in the liquid

visual.alt: Ideal solution of A and B: the partial pressure of A falls in a straight line from 24 kPa to zero, that of B rises in a straight line from zero to 64 kPa, and the total vapour pressure rises in a straight line from 24 to 64 kPa
visual.caption: Illustrative values: pure A 24 kPa, pure B 64 kPa at the same temperature.

slides.narration: Here is the picture for an ideal mixture. As the share of B rises, the partial pressure of A falls in a straight line to zero, and that of B rises in a straight line from zero. Their sum, the total vapour pressure, is another straight line from pure A to pure B. Any bending away from these lines means the solution is not ideal.

slides.heading: Worked example: composition of the vapour
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At $300\ \text{K}$ the vapour pressures of pure benzene and pure toluene are $13.8\ \text{kPa}$ and $4.6\ \text{kPa}$. A liquid contains $2\ \text{mol}$ benzene and $3\ \text{mol}$ toluene. Find the total vapour pressure and the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour (ideal solution).

**Step 1.** $x_\text{B} = 2 \div 5 = 0.40$; $x_\text{T} = 0.60$.

**Step 2.** $p_\text{B} = 13.8 \times 0.40 = 5.52\ \text{kPa}$; $p_\text{T} = 4.6 \times 0.60 = 2.76\ \text{kPa}$; $p_\text{total} = 8.28\ \text{kPa}$.

**Step 3.** $y_\text{B} = 5.52 \div 8.28 = 0.667$.

visual.alt: Table comparing the mole fractions of benzene and toluene in the liquid and the vapour

slides.narration: Benzene is two fifths of the liquid. Its partial pressure is thirteen point eight times nought point four, about five and a half kilopascal; toluene adds about two point eight. The total is a little over eight. In the vapour, benzene makes up two thirds, far more than its share of the liquid, because it is the more volatile liquid. Condensing this vapour and boiling it again enriches it further: that is fractional distillation.

slides.heading: Quick check: Raoult’s law
slides.body_md: Predict the vapour pressure or vapour composition of an ideal mixture.
slides.narration: Quick check. Multiply each pure vapour pressure by the mole fraction in the liquid, then add.

slides.heading: Non-volatile solutes and the link to Henry’s law
slides.body_md: For a **non-volatile solute** (sugar, urea), only the solvent contributes vapour: $p = p^\circ_1 x_1$, so the vapour pressure is **lowered**. Raoult’s law and Henry’s law have the same form, $p \propto x$; in Raoult’s law the constant is $p^\circ$, in Henry’s law it is $K_\text{H}$.

rows: A volatile component, usually the solvent

visual.alt: Table comparing Henry’s law and Raoult’s law

slides.narration: If the solute does not evaporate, as with sugar in water, only the solvent contributes vapour, and its vapour pressure is its pure value times its mole fraction. So adding a non-volatile solute always lowers the vapour pressure, an idea we build on in the next chapter. Notice too that Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law, in which the constant is simply the vapour pressure of the pure liquid.

slides.heading: Ideal and non-ideal solutions
slides.body_md: Whether a solution obeys Raoult’s law depends on how the **A–B attractions** compare with the A–A and B–B attractions.
columns: **Ideal** — obeys Raoult’s law at all compositions; A–B attractions about equal to A–A and B–B; $\Delta_\text{mix}H = 0$, $\Delta_\text{mix}V = 0$. Examples: n-hexane + n-heptane; benzene + toluene; bromoethane + chloroethane.

**Positive deviation** — A–B attractions **weaker**; vapour pressure higher; $\Delta_\text{mix}H > 0$, volume increases. Examples: ethanol + water, acetone + carbon disulfide.

**Negative deviation** — A–B attractions **stronger**; vapour pressure lower; $\Delta_\text{mix}H < 0$, volume decreases. Examples: chloroform + acetone, nitric acid + water.

visual.alt: Table of ideal solutions and solutions with positive and negative deviation

slides.narration: Why do some mixtures break Raoult’s law? It is about attractions. If A and B attract each other as strongly as they attract themselves, the solution is ideal, with no heat or volume change on mixing. If the new attractions are weaker, molecules escape more easily, giving positive deviation. If they are stronger, as when chloroform forms hydrogen bonds with acetone, molecules are held back, giving negative deviation and warming.

slides.heading: Deviations on a graph
slides.body_md: Positive deviation: total vapour pressure lies **above** the Raoult line. Negative deviation: it lies **below** it.

x.label: Mole fraction of B in the liquid

visual.alt: Total vapour pressure against composition: the ideal straight line from 24 to 64 kPa, a curve bulging above it for positive deviation and a curve sagging below it for negative deviation
visual.caption: Illustrative curves. A large enough deviation gives a maximum or a minimum in total pressure: an azeotrope.

slides.narration: On a graph the difference is easy to see. The straight line is the ideal prediction. A curve that bulges above it shows positive deviation, because molecules escape more easily than expected. A curve that sags below it shows negative deviation. If the bulge or the sag is large enough, the curve passes through a maximum or a minimum.

slides.heading: Worked example: deciding the deviation from data
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Liquids X ($p^\circ = 30\ \text{kPa}$) and Y ($p^\circ = 70\ \text{kPa}$) are mixed with $x_\text{X} = 0.25$. The measured vapour pressure is $52\ \text{kPa}$. Is the solution ideal? What would you expect for the temperature and volume on mixing?

**Step 1.** Raoult: $p = 30 \times 0.25 + 70 \times 0.75 = 7.5 + 52.5 = 60\ \text{kPa}$.

**Step 2.** Measured $52 < 60$: **negative deviation**.

**Step 3.** X–Y attractions are stronger: the mixture warms ($\Delta_\text{mix}H < 0$) and contracts ($\Delta_\text{mix}V < 0$).

visual.alt: Table comparing predicted and measured vapour pressure for the worked example

slides.narration: First work out what Raoult’s law predicts: seven and a half plus fifty two and a half, sixty kilopascal. The measured value is only fifty two, lower than predicted, so molecules are being held back by stronger attractions between X and Y. That is negative deviation, and we would expect the mixture to warm up and to occupy a little less volume than the two liquids separately.

slides.heading: Quick check: identify the deviation
slides.body_md: Two liquids cool when mixed and the mixture’s volume is slightly greater than the sum of the volumes. What kind of deviation is this?
slides.narration: Quick check. Cooling on mixing means heat is absorbed, so some attractions are being lost.

slides.heading: Azeotropes
slides.body_md: An **azeotrope** (constant-boiling mixture) boils at a constant temperature with the **same composition in liquid and vapour**. Large **positive** deviation gives a **minimum-boiling** azeotrope; large **negative** deviation gives a **maximum-boiling** azeotrope.

rows: Ethanol + water: about 95% ethanol by volume, boils near 351 K
Nitric acid + water: about 68% HNO₃ by mass, boils near 393.5 K
Hydrochloric acid + water: about 20% HCl by mass, boils near 383 K

visual.alt: Table of minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes with examples

slides.narration: Some mixtures boil like a single pure liquid: the vapour has exactly the same composition as the liquid. These are azeotropes. A large positive deviation makes the vapour pressure pass through a maximum, so the boiling point passes through a minimum: ethanol and water is the famous example. A large negative deviation, as with nitric acid and water, gives a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

slides.heading: Boiling point–composition diagram
slides.body_md: For a minimum-boiling azeotrope, the liquid and vapour curves meet at a **minimum**. On fractional distillation, the vapour at the top of the column approaches the **azeotrope**, and the residue approaches the pure component on the other side of it — never both pure components.

x.label: Mole fraction of B (the more volatile liquid)

visual.alt: Boiling temperature against composition for a minimum-boiling azeotrope: the liquid curve and the vapour curve fall from the boiling point of pure A and meet at a minimum near a mole fraction of B of nine tenths, just below the boiling point of pure B
visual.caption: Illustrative curves. At the minimum the liquid and vapour have the same composition.

slides.narration: This diagram plots boiling temperature against composition. The lower curve shows where liquid of each composition starts to boil; the upper curve shows the vapour that forms. They meet at a minimum, the azeotrope. Starting from a dilute mixture, each evaporation and condensation in a fractionating column moves the vapour towards the azeotrope, but never past it. So distillation gives the azeotrope at the top, not the pure liquid.

slides.heading: Worked example: what does distillation give?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A distiller fractionally distils a 20% (by volume) ethanol–water mixture. What collects at the top of the column? (b) A chemist distils dilute nitric acid (20% by mass). What is left in the flask at the end?

**(a)** The minimum-boiling azeotrope, about 95% ethanol, distils over; it boils lower than either pure liquid, so pure ethanol cannot be obtained this way.

**(b)** Water (lower boiling) distils first; the residue moves towards the maximum-boiling azeotrope, about 68% nitric acid, which then distils unchanged.

visual.alt: Table of distillation outcomes for the two azeotropic mixtures

slides.narration: Use the type of azeotrope. Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope, so it is the lowest boiling thing present: it distils over, and pure ethanol never appears at the top. Nitric acid and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope, the highest boiling thing present, so water distils away first and the acid left behind becomes more concentrated until it reaches about sixty eight percent.

sections.heading: 1. Types of solutions
sections.body_md: A **solution** is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The component in larger amount is the **solvent**; the others are **solutes**. By the states of solvent and solute there are nine types: gaseous (air; humid air; camphor in air), liquid (soda water; ethanol in water; salt solution) and **solid solutions** (hydrogen in palladium; sodium amalgam; alloys such as brass, bronze and carat gold). A **binary** solution has two components.

key_terms.definition_md: A homogeneous mixture of two or more components.
A solution in which the solvent is a solid, e.g. an alloy such as brass.

sections.heading: 2. Concentration terms
sections.body_md:
- **Mass %** $= \dfrac{\text{mass of component}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$; **volume %**; **w/v %** (g per 100 mL).
- **ppm** $= \dfrac{\text{mass of component}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 10^{6}$ (1 ppm = 1 mg per kg).
- **Mole fraction** $x_\text{B} = n_\text{B}/(n_\text{A} + n_\text{B})$; $\sum x = 1$.
- **Molarity** $M$ = mol of solute per L of **solution**; **molality** $m$ = mol of solute per kg of **solvent**.
- **Normality** $N$ = gram equivalents of solute per L of solution; equivalent mass = molar mass ÷ n-factor (basicity, acidity, electrons transferred), so $N = n \times M$. At an end point, $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$.
- Mass %, ppm, mole fraction and molality are **independent of temperature**; molarity and normality fall slightly on heating because the volume of solution increases.
- Conversions: assume 100 g of solution for a percentage; use density to get volume; molarity ↔ molality: $m = \dfrac{1000M}{1000d - M M_\text{B}}$ (d in g mL⁻¹, $M_\text{B}$ = molar mass of solute).

key_terms.definition_md: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; independent of temperature.
Number of gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution.
Molar mass divided by the n-factor of the substance in the reaction.

sections.heading: 3. Solubility of gases; Henry’s law
sections.body_md:
Solubility of a gas in a liquid increases with **pressure** and decreases with **temperature** (dissolving is usually exothermic).

**Henry’s law:** at constant temperature, the solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure; $p = K_\text{H}\,x$. Larger $K_\text{H}$ → less soluble; $K_\text{H}$ increases with temperature.

**Applications:** soft drinks bottled under high CO₂ pressure; the bends in divers (tanks use air diluted with helium); anoxia at high altitude; low oxygen in warm water.

**Limitations:** holds for low pressures, gases that do not react with or dissociate in the solvent (not NH₃ or HCl in water), and dilute solutions.

key_terms.definition_md: At constant temperature the partial pressure of a gas over a solution is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

sections.heading: 4. Raoult’s law; ideal and non-ideal solutions
sections.body_md:
**Raoult’s law:** for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component equals its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction: $p_\text{A} = p^\circ_\text{A}x_\text{A}$; $p_\text{total} = p_\text{A} + p_\text{B}$ (Dalton). Vapour composition: $y_\text{A} = p_\text{A}/p_\text{total}$; the vapour is richer in the more volatile component. For a **non-volatile solute**, $p = p^\circ_1 x_1$ (vapour pressure lowered). Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law with $K_\text{H} = p^\circ$.

| | Ideal | Positive deviation | Negative deviation |
|---|---|---|---|
| A–B forces | ≈ A–A, B–B | weaker | stronger |
| Vapour pressure | as Raoult | higher | lower |
| $\Delta_\text{mix}H$ | 0 | > 0 | < 0 |
| $\Delta_\text{mix}V$ | 0 | > 0 | < 0 |
| Examples | hexane + heptane; benzene + toluene | ethanol + water; acetone + CS₂ | chloroform + acetone; HNO₃ + water |

key_terms.definition_md: A solution that obeys Raoult’s law at all compositions, with zero enthalpy and volume of mixing.

sections.heading: 5. Azeotropes and fractional distillation
sections.body_md:
An **azeotrope** is a liquid mixture that boils at constant temperature and distils with unchanged composition (liquid and vapour have the same composition).
- **Minimum-boiling azeotrope:** from large positive deviation; e.g. ethanol + water (about 95% ethanol by volume, about 351 K).
- **Maximum-boiling azeotrope:** from large negative deviation; e.g. nitric acid + water (about 68% HNO₃, about 393.5 K), HCl + water (about 20% HCl, about 383 K).

**Boiling point–composition diagrams:** the liquid and vapour curves meet at the azeotrope (minimum or maximum). Fractional distillation of a mixture gives one pure component and the azeotrope — never both pure components — because at the azeotrope the vapour has the same composition as the liquid.

key_terms.definition_md: A constant-boiling mixture whose vapour has the same composition as the liquid.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Dividing by the mass of solution instead of the mass of solvent for molality.
- Treating 1 M H₂SO₄ as 1 N (it is 2 N).
- Saying a larger Henry’s constant means a more soluble gas.
- Using liquid mole fractions for the vapour instead of y = pA/ptotal.
- Linking positive deviation with a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Numericals: formula, substitution with units, and a final answer with correct units (full working expected).
- Deviation questions: the change in intermolecular forces plus the signs of ΔmixH and ΔmixV, with an example.
- Azeotrope questions: type, cause, an example, and a labelled boiling point–composition sketch.

questions.stem_md: A jeweller’s 18-carat gold contains gold with copper and silver uniformly mixed. It is best described as:

options.text_md: a colloid of copper in gold
a solid solution in which gold is the solvent

questions.solution_md: Gold (75%) is the major component and the mixture is uniform, so it is a solid solution with gold as solvent — option (d).

questions.solution_md: True. Mercury (a liquid) is dissolved in solid sodium.

questions.stem_md: Give one example each of (a) a solution of a gas in a liquid and (b) a solid solution of a solid in a solid. Name the solute and the solvent in each.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of concentration terms both stay unchanged when a solution is warmed from 15 °C to 35 °C?

questions.stem_md: What is the normality of a 0.3 M solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂?
questions.solution_md: Ca(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻ per formula unit, so N = 2 × 0.3 = 0.6 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Concentrated nitric acid used in the laboratory is 63% HNO₃ by mass and has a density of 1.40 g mL⁻¹ (M = 63). Calculate (a) its molarity and (b) its molality.

answer.model_answer_md:
Take $100\ \text{g}$ of acid: $63\ \text{g}$ HNO₃ $= 1.0\ \text{mol}$; water $= 37\ \text{g}$. Volume $= 100 \div 1.40 = 71.4\ \text{mL}$.

(a) Molarity $= 1.0 \div 0.0714 = 14.0\ \text{M}$.

(b) Molality $= 1.0 \div 0.037 = 27.0\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A solution is made by dissolving 18 g of glucose (M = 180) in 162 g of water. Calculate (a) the mass percentage of glucose, (b) the mole fraction of glucose and (c) the molality of the solution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mass % $= 18 \div 180 \times 100 = 10\%$ (total mass 180 g).

(b) $n_\text{glucose} = 0.10$; $n_\text{water} = 162 \div 18 = 9.0$; $x = 0.10 \div 9.10 = 0.011$.

(c) Molality $= 0.10 \div 0.162 = 0.617\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: What volume of 0.25 N sulfuric acid is needed to neutralise exactly 2.0 g of sodium hydroxide (M = 40)? What would the molarity of this acid be?

answer.model_answer_md: Equivalents of NaOH $= 2.0 \div 40 = 0.050$. At neutralisation, equivalents of acid $= 0.050$, so $V = 0.050 \div 0.25 = 0.20\ \text{L} = 200\ \text{mL}$. Sulfuric acid has n-factor 2, so its molarity $= 0.25 \div 2 = 0.125\ \text{M}$.

(b) 4.9 g of sulfuric acid (M = 98) is dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution. Calculate its molarity and normality. [1½]

(c) The density of this solution is 1.02 g mL⁻¹. Calculate its molality. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Molality: moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Normality: gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution. ppm: parts by mass of a component per $10^6$ parts by mass of solution.

(b) Moles $= 4.9 \div 98 = 0.050$; molarity $= 0.050 \div 0.500 = 0.10\ \text{M}$; normality $= 2 \times 0.10 = 0.20\ \text{N}$.

(c) Mass of solution $= 500 \times 1.02 = 510\ \text{g}$; water $= 510 - 4.9 = 505.1\ \text{g}$; molality $= 0.050 \div 0.5051 = 0.099\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; 0.10 M, 0.20 N; 0.099 mol/kg.

questions.stem_md: At 293 K the Henry’s law constants (in kbar) of four gases in water are: argon 40.3, methane 41.9, ethane 30.6, helium 145. Which gas is the least soluble in water at the same partial pressure?
questions.solution_md: x = p ÷ KH, so the largest KH gives the smallest mole fraction — option (a).

questions.stem_md: When an aqueous solution of oxygen is warmed at constant partial pressure of oxygen, its solubility:

options.text_md: increases, because the Henry’s law constant increases
decreases, because the Henry’s law constant decreases
does not change, because pressure is constant
decreases, because the Henry’s law constant increases

questions.solution_md: KH rises with temperature, so x = p ÷ KH falls — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Ammonia does not obey Henry’s law in water mainly because:

options.text_md: it reacts with water to form ammonium and hydroxide ions
it has a very large Henry’s law constant

questions.solution_md: Henry’s law holds for gases that do not react with or ionise in the solvent — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Soft drinks are bottled under a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of about 4 bar. If the same drink were bottled under 2 bar at the same temperature, the dissolved carbon dioxide would be:
questions.solution_md: By Henry’s law the amount dissolved is proportional to the partial pressure — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Henry’s law constant of a gas in water increases as the temperature rises.
questions.solution_md: True. A larger KH at higher temperature means a lower solubility of the gas.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogen chloride does not obey Henry’s law in water.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen chloride is a non-polar molecule.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (HCl ionises in water); R is false — HCl is polar — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Nitrogen is present in air at a partial pressure of $0.78\ \text{bar}$. With $K_\text{H}(\ce{N2}) = 76.48\ \text{kbar}$ at $293\ \text{K}$, how many millimoles of nitrogen dissolve in $1.0\ \text{kg}$ of water?
Use Henry’s law to explain why soft drinks are bottled under high pressure, and why a warm bottle loses its fizz faster than a cold one once opened.

answer.model_answer_md: High pressure of carbon dioxide above the drink increases its solubility, so more gas is dissolved; when the bottle is opened the pressure falls and gas comes out. Henry’s constant increases with temperature, so a warm drink can hold less carbon dioxide and loses it faster.

questions.solution_md: Pressure raises solubility; temperature raises KH.

marking_scheme.step: High pressure → more CO₂ dissolved; released on opening
Higher temperature → larger KH → less CO₂ held

questions.stem_md: State two conditions under which Henry’s law is obeyed, and explain why it does not apply to ammonia dissolving in water.

answer.model_answer_md: Henry’s law holds at low pressure (and not too low temperature), for dilute solutions, and for gases that do not react with or dissociate in the solvent. Ammonia reacts with water (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻), so much more dissolves than the law predicts.

questions.solution_md: Conditions; reaction with water.

questions.stem_md: Carbon dioxide is held above 1.0 kg of water at a partial pressure of 3.34 bar at 298 K (KH = 1.67 kbar). (a) Calculate the mass of CO₂ dissolved. (b) How would the mass change if the water were at 318 K? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $x = 3.34 \div 1670 = 0.0020$; moles of water $= 1000 \div 18 = 55.56$; $n_{\ce{CO2}} \approx 0.0020 \times 55.56 = 0.111\ \text{mol}$; mass $= 0.111 \times 44 = 4.89\ \text{g}$.

(b) Less CO₂ would dissolve, because $K_\text{H}$ increases with temperature (dissolving the gas is exothermic).

questions.solution_md: 4.89 g; less at 318 K.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Henry’s law and give two of its applications in daily life. [2]

(b) At 293 K, KH for oxygen in water is 34.86 kbar. Calculate the mole fraction of oxygen in water in equilibrium with (i) air, in which the partial pressure of oxygen is 0.21 bar, and (ii) pure oxygen at 1.0 bar. By what factor does breathing pure oxygen raise the amount of dissolved oxygen? [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is proportional to the partial pressure of the gas: $p = K_\text{H}x$. Applications: soft drinks bottled under high CO₂ pressure; divers’ tanks filled with air diluted with helium to reduce the bends (or anoxia at high altitude).

(b) (i) $x = 0.21 \div 34860 = 6.02 \times 10^{-6}$. (ii) $x = 1.0 \div 34860 = 2.87 \times 10^{-5}$. Factor $= 1.0 \div 0.21 = 4.76$ (the ratio of the two partial pressures).

questions.solution_md: Law and applications; 6.02 × 10⁻⁶, 2.87 × 10⁻⁵, factor 4.76.

questions.stem_md: Liquids A (p° = 60 kPa) and B (p° = 20 kPa) form an ideal solution. What is the vapour pressure of a solution containing equal numbers of moles of A and B?
Two liquids cool when mixed, and the volume of the mixture is slightly greater than the sum of their volumes. The solution:

options.text_md: shows negative deviation from Raoult’s law
shows positive deviation from Raoult’s law

questions.solution_md: Heat absorbed and expansion mean A–B attractions are weaker, so molecules escape more easily: positive deviation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A mixture of n-hexane and n-heptane behaves almost ideally. Which statement about the mixing of these two liquids is correct?
questions.solution_md: In an ideal solution A–B attractions equal A–A and B–B, so there is no heat or volume change on mixing — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A nearly ideal liquid mixture contains equal moles of benzene (more volatile) and toluene (less volatile). Compared with the liquid, the vapour in equilibrium with it is:
questions.solution_md: yA = pA ÷ ptotal; the more volatile component has the larger partial pressure, so it is enriched in the vapour — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of liquids shows negative deviation from Raoult’s law?
questions.solution_md: Strong attractions between HNO₃ and water lower the vapour pressure — option (c). Ethanol–water and acetone–CS₂ show positive deviation; benzene–toluene is nearly ideal.

questions.stem_md: The vapour pressure of pure water at a certain temperature is 30 kPa. What is the vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute in which the mole fraction of water is 0.90?
questions.solution_md: p = p° x(water) = 30 × 0.90 = 27 kPa — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State Raoult’s law for a solution of two volatile liquids. Show that Raoult’s law is a special case of Henry’s law.

answer.model_answer_md: In a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component equals the vapour pressure of the pure component multiplied by its mole fraction: pA = p°A xA. Henry’s law has the same form, p = KH x; Raoult’s law is the special case in which the constant KH equals the vapour pressure of the pure component, p°.

questions.solution_md: Statement; KH = p°.

questions.stem_md: When 20 mL of chloroform is mixed with 20 mL of acetone, the mixture becomes warm and its volume is a little less than 40 mL. Explain both observations and name the type of deviation from Raoult’s law.

answer.model_answer_md: Chloroform forms hydrogen bonds with the oxygen of acetone (Cl₃C–H···O=C), which are stronger than the attractions in the pure liquids. Forming these bonds releases heat (ΔmixH < 0) and draws the molecules closer (ΔmixV < 0). The vapour pressure is lower than predicted: negative deviation.

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen bonding; negative deviation.

marking_scheme.step: Stronger A–B attraction (H-bonding) explains warming and contraction

questions.stem_md: Liquids A (p° = 80 kPa) and B (p° = 30 kPa) form an ideal solution whose total vapour pressure is 55 kPa at the same temperature. Calculate (a) the mole fraction of A in the liquid and (b) the mole fraction of A in the vapour.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $p = p^\circ_\text{B} + (p^\circ_\text{A} - p^\circ_\text{B})x_\text{A}$: $55 = 30 + 50x_\text{A}$, so $x_\text{A} = 0.50$.

(b) $p_\text{A} = 80 \times 0.50 = 40\ \text{kPa}$; $y_\text{A} = 40 \div 55 = 0.727$.

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between an ideal solution and a solution showing negative deviation from Raoult’s law.

answer.model_answer_md: An ideal solution obeys Raoult’s law at all compositions, while a solution with negative deviation has a lower vapour pressure than the law predicts. In an ideal solution A–B attractions equal A–A and B–B attractions; with negative deviation they are stronger. For an ideal solution ΔmixH = 0 and ΔmixV = 0; with negative deviation ΔmixH < 0 (heat is released) and ΔmixV < 0 (contraction).

questions.solution_md: Vapour pressure, forces, ΔH and ΔV.

questions.stem_md: Sketch and explain the graph of total vapour pressure against mole fraction for (a) an ideal solution and (b) a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult’s law. Give one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) For an ideal solution, the total vapour pressure is a straight line joining the vapour pressures of the pure liquids; each partial pressure is also a straight line. Example: n-hexane + n-heptane. (b) For positive deviation, the total vapour pressure curve lies above the straight line, often passing through a maximum, because weaker A–B attractions let molecules escape more easily. Example: ethanol + water.

questions.solution_md: Straight line vs curve above.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Curve above the line and example

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A mixture of benzene and toluene behaves almost as an ideal solution.

**Reason (R):** Benzene has a higher vapour pressure than toluene at the same temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A; the mixture is ideal because benzene–toluene attractions are very similar to those in the pure liquids — option (b).

questions.stem_md: At 320 K, the vapour pressures of pure liquids A and B are 50 kPa and 20 kPa. For an ideal solution with a mole fraction of A of 0.30, calculate the mole fraction of A in the vapour.
questions.solution_md: $p_\text{A} = 50 \times 0.30 = 15\ \text{kPa}$; $p_\text{B} = 20 \times 0.70 = 14\ \text{kPa}$; $p_\text{total} = 29\ \text{kPa}$; $y_\text{A} = 15 \div 29 = 0.517$.

questions.stem_md: Match each pair of liquids (hexane–heptane, ethanol–water, nitric acid–water, chloroform–acetone) with the description that fits it best.

match_right.text_md: Hydrogen bonds form between the two components

questions.solution_md: Hexane–heptane → nearly ideal; ethanol–water → minimum-boiling azeotrope (about 95% ethanol); HNO₃–water → maximum-boiling azeotrope (about 68% acid); chloroform–acetone → C–H···O hydrogen bonds (negative deviation).

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Raoult’s law and derive an expression for the total vapour pressure of an ideal solution of two volatile liquids A and B in terms of the mole fraction of B. [2]

(b) Pure liquids A and B have vapour pressures of 90 kPa and 36 kPa at 300 K. An ideal solution of A and B has a total vapour pressure of 54 kPa at this temperature. Calculate the mole fraction of A in the liquid and in the vapour. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The partial vapour pressure of each volatile component equals its pure vapour pressure times its mole fraction: $p_\text{A} = p^\circ_\text{A}x_\text{A}$, $p_\text{B} = p^\circ_\text{B}x_\text{B}$. By Dalton’s law $p = p_\text{A} + p_\text{B} = p^\circ_\text{A}(1 - x_\text{B}) + p^\circ_\text{B}x_\text{B} = p^\circ_\text{A} + (p^\circ_\text{B} - p^\circ_\text{A})x_\text{B}$.

(b) $54 = 36 + (90 - 36)x_\text{A}$, so $x_\text{A} = 18 \div 54 = 0.333$. $p_\text{A} = 90 \times 0.333 = 30\ \text{kPa}$; $y_\text{A} = 30 \div 54 = 0.556$.

questions.solution_md: Derivation; xA = 0.333; yA = 0.556.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are positive and negative deviations from Raoult’s law? Explain each in terms of intermolecular forces, giving the signs of ΔmixH and ΔmixV and one example of each. [3]

(b) What is an azeotrope? Why cannot the components of an azeotrope be separated by fractional distillation? [2]

answer.model_answer_md: In positive deviation, the vapour pressure is higher than Raoult’s law predicts, because A–B attractions are weaker than A–A and B–B; mixing absorbs heat (ΔmixH > 0) and the volume increases (ΔmixV > 0). Example: ethanol + water. In negative deviation, the vapour pressure is lower, because A–B attractions are stronger; mixing releases heat (ΔmixH < 0) and the volume decreases (ΔmixV < 0). Example: chloroform + acetone. An azeotrope is a liquid mixture that boils at a constant temperature and distils without change in composition. At the azeotropic composition the vapour has exactly the same composition as the liquid, so repeated evaporation and condensation cannot change the composition.

questions.solution_md: Deviations with forces, signs and examples; azeotrope.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Positive deviation with signs and example
(a) Negative deviation with signs and example

questions.stem_md: A pair of liquids shows a large positive deviation from Raoult’s law. Its azeotrope will:

options.text_md: boil at a higher temperature than either pure liquid
boil between the two boiling points
boil at a lower temperature than either pure liquid

questions.solution_md: Positive deviation raises the vapour pressure, giving a minimum-boiling azeotrope — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Dilute hydrochloric acid (5% HCl) is boiled in an open flask for a long time. The acid left in the flask approaches about 20% HCl because:

options.text_md: HCl and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope
HCl is less volatile than water at all compositions
HCl and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope of about that composition
water and HCl form an ideal solution

questions.solution_md: Water boils away first and the residue moves to the maximum-boiling azeotrope — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Rectified spirit (about 95% ethanol in water) is a constant-boiling mixture. Which statement about such an azeotropic mixture is correct?

options.text_md: Its liquid and vapour have the same composition at the boiling point
Its boiling point changes during distillation
It can be separated by fractional distillation

questions.solution_md: Equal compositions of liquid and vapour are why the mixture distils unchanged — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a boiling point–composition diagram for a pair of liquids, the liquid and vapour curves touch at a minimum in the middle of the diagram. This shows:

options.text_md: a maximum-boiling azeotrope formed by a large negative deviation
a minimum-boiling azeotrope formed by a large positive deviation

questions.solution_md: A minimum in boiling point corresponds to a maximum in vapour pressure, i.e. positive deviation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A liquid mixture that boils at a constant temperature and distils without any change in composition is called an ___.
questions.solution_md: An **azeotrope** (constant-boiling mixture).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pure ethanol can be obtained by fractional distillation of a mixture of ethanol and water.

**Reason (R):** Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false — the azeotrope (about 95% ethanol) distils over and pure ethanol is not obtained; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Rectified spirit contains about 95% ethanol. Why can it not be converted into pure ethanol by fractional distillation? Name the type of azeotrope involved.

answer.model_answer_md: Ethanol and water show large positive deviation and form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95% ethanol. At this composition the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so distillation cannot change it any further.

questions.solution_md: Minimum-boiling azeotrope; same composition of liquid and vapour.

marking_scheme.step: Liquid and vapour of the same composition

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between minimum-boiling and maximum-boiling azeotropes, stating the kind of deviation that produces each and one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A minimum-boiling azeotrope boils at a lower temperature than either component; it arises from large positive deviation (higher vapour pressure), e.g. ethanol + water (about 95% ethanol). A maximum-boiling azeotrope boils at a higher temperature than either component; it arises from large negative deviation (lower vapour pressure), e.g. nitric acid + water (about 68% HNO₃).

questions.solution_md: Boiling behaviour, deviation, example.

questions.stem_md: Predict what collects as distillate and what remains in the flask when each mixture is fractionally distilled, giving reasons: (a) 30% (by volume) ethanol in water; (b) 10% (by mass) hydrochloric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Ethanol–water forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope (about 95% ethanol), the lowest-boiling mixture possible, so the azeotrope distils over and water remains in the flask. (b) HCl–water forms a maximum-boiling azeotrope (about 20% HCl). Since 10% is below this, water (lower boiling) distils over first, and the residue becomes richer in HCl until it reaches the azeotrope, which then distils unchanged.

questions.solution_md: (a) azeotrope distils, water left; (b) water distils, residue → 20% HCl.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled boiling point–composition diagram for a pair of liquids that forms a maximum-boiling azeotrope, and explain what it shows. [2]

(b) Nitric acid and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope at about 68% HNO₃. Predict what happens when (i) 40% nitric acid and (ii) 80% nitric acid are fractionally distilled. Explain your answers. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The diagram plots boiling temperature against composition. The liquid (lower) and vapour (upper) curves rise from the boiling points of the pure liquids and meet at a maximum at the azeotropic composition; there liquid and vapour have the same composition. (b) (i) 40% is on the water-rich side of the azeotrope. The vapour is richer in water, so water distils over and the residue becomes more concentrated in acid until it reaches about 68% HNO₃, which then distils unchanged. (ii) 80% is on the acid-rich side; here the vapour is richer in HNO₃, so nitric acid distils over first and the residue becomes more dilute, again approaching 68%. In neither case can both pure components be obtained.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; residue tends to the azeotrope from both sides.
